Chapter Four: Learning by Doing—The Importance of Direct Practice
So, now that we’ve talked about focus, let’s take a look at the next big principle—directness, or learning by actually doing the thing you want to master.
Think about it: so much of traditional learning is passive. You read, you listen, maybe you watch someone else. Sure, those things can help, but they often leave you feeling unprepared when it’s time to take action in the real world.
Ultralearning flips that approach. It says, hey, if you want to learn something for real, you’ve gotta practice in the same context, and in the same way, you’ll actually use that skill.
There’s a name for this— transfer-appropriate practice. It’s a simple idea: the closer your practice is to the real thing, the more effective your learning will be.
Picture someone trying to learn a new language. Sure, memorizing vocabulary lists is useful, but if you really want to make fast progress, nothing beats having real conversations with native speakers.
Or take a programmer. You can read all about code, but you’ll learn a whole lot more by actually building projects—by getting your hands dirty.
I like to think of directness as a bridge between learning and performing. The shorter and sturdier that bridge, the easier it is to carry what you’ve learned into real life.
But here’s the catch: if your practice is too abstract or disconnected from your goal, it’s tough to make that leap when it matters most.
So, how do you put directness into action?
Try these strategies:
Project-based learning: Design projects that feel like real-world challenges—maybe building a website, writing an article, or even performing on stage.
Immersion: Surround yourself with the skill or environment you’re aiming for. That could mean living in a country where the language is spoken, or working right alongside experts.
Simulation: Create scenarios that mimic the real thing, with all the pressures and constraints you’d actually face.
Now, I won’t sugarcoat it—direct practice can be uncomfortable. It shines a light on what you don’t know and makes you face your mistakes head-on.
But you know what? That discomfort is a good sign. It means you’re making real, meaningful progress. By diving into the actual task, again and again, you start building real confidence—and real competence—that passive studying just can’t give you.
There’s a trap a lot of us fall into: waiting to feel “ready” before we start practicing directly. It’s easy to keep preparing, thinking you’ll avoid mistakes that way.
But honestly, true readiness only comes from doing the work, making those mistakes, and learning as you go.
Directness also helps you dodge the illusion of competence. You might feel like you know a lot after reading or watching tutorials, but it’s only when you put it into practice that you see what you’ve really learned—and where you still need to grow.
So, here’s the key takeaway: directness is all about closing the gap between learning and doing. When you focus on real-world practice, you don’t just move faster—you build skills that are strong, flexible, and ready for anything life throws your way.
